1.title: Mandatum: what it is
1.text:
Lesson of 9 December 2026 (Obligations; mandatum). Source: Benke/Meissel, Roman Law of Obligations, ch. VIII, pp. 203–215 (page numbers below refer to this book unless 'Property' is added).

### Definition
In a MANDATUM the agent (MANDATARIUS) undertakes to carry out, FREE OF CHARGE, a legal or a factual act for the principal (MANDATOR) (p. 203). A legal act is, for example, standing surety for the mandator; a factual act is, for example, putting up a statue in his honour (p. 204).

### Characteristics
| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Consensual | Formed by agreement alone (p. 203); one of the four consensual contracts with sale, LOCATIO CONDUCTIO and SOCIETAS (p. 14). Although 'to mandate' sounds like 'to order', it is not a one-sided command. |
| Gratuitous | No fee. Reimbursing expenses is not consideration, so the mandate stays gratuitous. If a fee is agreed, it is a contract for work, not a mandate (p. 20). |
| Imperfectly bilateral | The mandator always has a claim to performance; claims of the mandatarius can, but need not, arise (p. 203). |
| BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM | The INTENTIO of the action refers to OPORTERE EX FIDE BONA (p. 204). |
| Among friends | Undertaken out of social convention, not for gain; the sources often cite AMICITIA (p. 204). |

### Ending the mandate
Agreement is needed not only to form the contract but also to continue it. Either party can end it by a unilateral declaration as long as there is RES INTEGRA, i.e. ending it still causes neither side any reliance loss (p. 203). (The study notes are unsure which Latin label goes with which side; the usual usage is REVOCATIO by the mandator, RENUNTIATIO by the mandatarius.)

### It must be someone else's affair
• Purely in the mandatarius' OWN interest = no binding mandate, only non-binding advice, CONSILIUM. The sources call it MANDATUM TUA GRATIA, which is misleading (p. 204; Gaius D 17.1.2.6, Case 174/1).
• In the COMMON interest of both = can be a mandate, but the mandatarius manages another's affair only insofar as the mandator's interest differs from his own (p. 205; see model exegesis 1).

terms.def: Consensual contract by which the MANDATARIUS undertakes to carry out, free of charge, a legal or factual act for the MANDATOR (Benke/Meissel, Obligations p. 203).
Situation in which ending the mandate still causes neither side any reliance loss; until then either party can end it unilaterally (p. 203).
A 'mandate' purely in the agent's own interest; in truth non-binding advice (CONSILIUM), not a contract (p. 204).

cards.q: What is a MANDATUM?
cards.a:
A consensual contract: the MANDATARIUS undertakes to carry out, FREE OF CHARGE, a legal or factual act for the MANDATOR.
• Legal act: e.g. standing surety for him
• Factual act: e.g. putting up a statue in his honour (pp. 203–204)

cards.q: What are the main characteristics of the mandate as a contract?
cards.a:
Consensual, gratuitous, imperfectly bilateral, BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM.
• Formed by agreement alone; a 'transaction among friends' (AMICITIA)
• INTENTIO: OPORTERE EX FIDE BONA (pp. 203–204)

cards.q: Why is a mandate called 'imperfectly bilateral'?
cards.a:
The mandator always has a claim to performance; the mandatarius' counterclaims (expenses, losses) can, but need not, arise.
• If no expenses arise, the mandator owes nothing (pp. 19, 203)

cards.q: A agrees to do a task for B and B promises a fee. Is this still a mandate?
cards.a:
No. An agreed fee is consideration, so it is a contract for work (LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS), not a mandate.
• Reimbursement of expenses is NOT consideration: a mandate stays gratuitous (p. 20)

cards.q: Until when can a mandate be ended unilaterally, and why at all?
cards.a:
As long as there is RES INTEGRA, i.e. ending it still causes neither side reliance loss.
• Agreement is needed to form AND to continue the mandate (p. 203)

cards.q: What is a MANDATUM TUA GRATIA?
cards.a:
A 'mandate' purely in the agent's own interest: in truth non-binding advice (CONSILIUM), no contract, no liability.
• Gaius D 17.1.2.6 (Case 174/1); the name is misleading (p. 204)

cards.q: Can a transaction in the common interest of mandator and mandatarius be a mandate?
cards.a:
Yes, but the mandatarius manages another's affair only insofar as the mandator's interest differs from his own (p. 205).
• Ulpian (Celsus) D 17.1.16 (Case 175): costs recoverable only beyond the increase in value of his own land

2.title: Property law you need for mandate
2.text:
A mandate creates only OBLIGATIONS between mandator and mandatarius: an OBLIGATIO is a personal bond with effects only between creditor and debtor (p. 212). WHO becomes possessor or owner of the thing the mandatarius buys, sells or collects is decided by property law.

### 1. Indirect agency is the classical rule
In pre-classical and classical law a person SUI IURIS generally cannot acquire possession for someone else (Property p. 48; Gai. 2.95, Case 32). So the mandatarius acquires FIRST, in his own name, and transfers to the mandator in a SECOND, separate act. Example 65 (p. 205): Achilles undertakes to buy a thing from Drakon for Pomona. Drakon delivers it to Achilles by TRADITIO in Achilles' own name; Achilles then transfers possession and ownership to Pomona by a second TRADITIO. Until then Pomona has only her contractual claim (ACTIO MANDATI DIRECTA). Direct agency (the deal affects the principal immediately) was opened up generally only by Justinian (Property p. 49). The same holds for money: a PROCURATOR who collected his principal's debts as paying agent was himself possessor and owner of the money (Africanus (Julian) D 17.1.34 pr, Case 4, p. 45).

### 2. Exceptions: TUTOR, CURATOR, PROCURATOR
These persons SUI IURIS acquire directly for the person they act for. PROCURATORES were often freed slaves still bound to their former master (Property pp. 48–49). Slaves and sons acquire for the DOMINUS through IUSSUM or PECULIUM; a later approval (RATIHABITIO) counts as a prior IUSSUM: RATI ENIM HABITIO MANDATO COMPARATUR (Ulpian D 46.3.12.4, Property p. 47).

### 3. TRADITIO by someone authorised; NEMO PLUS IURIS
TRADITIO needs a transferor who is owner or has AUTHORITY OF DISPOSAL, transfer of possession and a IUSTA CAUSA (Property p. 84). NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET (Ulpian D 41.1.20 pr, p. 77). Transferring possession through an authorised SUI IURIS person was always possible (p. 49). Iavolenus D 39.5.25 (Case 68): T, authorised to give a thing to Titius in E's name, gives it in his OWN name. Titius gets possession but not ownership; against E's REI VINDICATIO he has the EXCEPTIO DOLI; T must answer to E for exceeding his authority (FURTUM) (pp. 85–86).

### 4. SUPERFICIES SOLO CEDIT
What is firmly built on land follows the land (Property p. 137). This matters in D 17.1.16.

terms.def: The agent acquires in his own name and then transfers to the principal in a separate act; the classical rule for persons SUI IURIS (Property p. 48; Obligations p. 205).
Steward or agent, often a freedman; by exception he acquires possession directly for his master (Property p. 49).
NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET: nobody can transfer more rights than he himself has (Ulpian D 41.1.20 pr; Property p. 77).

cards.q: In classical law, how does the mandator acquire a thing that his mandatarius buys for him?
cards.a:
By indirect agency: the mandatarius acquires it first in his own name, then transfers possession and ownership by a second TRADITIO.
• Example 65: Achilles buys from Drakon for Pomona (p. 205)
• Until then the mandator has only the ACTIO MANDATI DIRECTA

cards.q: Direct vs indirect agency — what is the difference?
cards.a:
Direct: the transaction immediately affects the principal; indirect: it affects the agent, who then transfers in a separate act.
• Classical law: persons SUI IURIS generally only indirect (Property p. 48)
• Justinian opened direct agency generally (p. 49)

cards.q: Which persons SUI IURIS could exceptionally acquire possession directly for another in classical law?
cards.a:
TUTOR (for his ward), CURATOR (for the person in his care) and PROCURATOR (for his master).
• PROCURATORES were often freedmen bound to their master (Property pp. 48–49)

cards.q: What are the three requirements of transfer of ownership by TRADITIO?
cards.a:
Ownership or authority of disposal of the transferor, transfer of possession, IUSTA CAUSA.
• NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET (Ulpian D 41.1.20 pr) (Property pp. 77, 84)

cards.q: Iavolenus D 39.5.25 (Case 68): T is to give E's thing to Titius in E's name but gives it in his own name. Result?
cards.a:
Titius gets possession but not ownership: T was not authorised to dispose in his own name.
• E's REI VINDICATIO fails against Titius' EXCEPTIO DOLI
• T answers to E for exceeding his authority (FURTUM) (Property pp. 85–86)

cards.q: Africanus (Julian) D 17.1.34 pr (Case 4): who owns the money a PROCURATOR collected from his principal's debtors?
cards.a:
The procurator himself: as paying agent he became possessor and owner of the money.
• So no DATIO (and no MUTUUM) when the principal later 'lends' it to him; Julian gives the ACTIO MANDATI instead, covering the agreed 6 % interest (pp. 44–45)

3.title: Duties, liability and the two actions
3.text:
### The two actions
| | ACTIO MANDATI DIRECTA | ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA |
|---|---|---|
| Who sues whom | Mandator v mandatarius | Mandatarius v mandator |
| Aim | Performance of the mandate and surrender of what the mandatarius obtained from the transaction (p. 203) | Expenses and losses incurred in executing the mandate; NEVER a fee (p. 204) |
| Available | Always | Only if such claims arise |

Both are BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA. Example 11 (p. 32): Solon, as Diana's mandatary, collects a debt of 700 for her and spends 120 on travel; by set-off Diana's claim against him shrinks to 580.

### Duties of the mandatarius
• Carry out the transaction as agreed, safeguarding the mandator's interests; e.g. hand over the thing bought (pp. 205–206).
• Secondary duties from BONA FIDES: protection, care, information. He must promptly tell the mandator if he cannot carry out the mandate (Gaius D 17.1.27.2, Case 185). Example 66: Laura, seriously ill, asks Xerxes to bring medicine from Greece; he breaks his leg and must tell her so that she can ask someone else (p. 206).
• Liability: as a rule only DOLUS and CULPA LATA, which fits a gratuitous act of friendship. Not telling Laura is CULPA LATA, so Xerxes is liable. Culpable non-performance: the mandator may claim his expectation interest (p. 206).
• Background, the principle of utility: liability follows the distribution of interests; whoever acts only for another's benefit is liable more mildly (p. 52).

### Duties of the mandator
• Expenses: only those incurred BONA FIDE in duly performing the mandate (Gaius D 17.1.27.4, Case 178). Example 67: Bellona is to deliver a message and hires a horse although riding was not agreed; the horse hire is not reimbursed (p. 207).
• Losses directly linked to the mandate, irrespective of fault: 'liability for risk' (p. 207). Reason: whoever benefits from the gratuitous performance should carry the risk of accidental harm (p. 208; Africanus (Julian) D 47.2.62(61).5, Case 181).
• Limit: losses from the general risk of life (robbery, shipwreck, illness) are not mandate-specific. Example 69: Orestes is robbed of 100 on his way with Elektra's message; no claim (Paulus D 17.1.26.6, Case 179; p. 208).
• Secondary duties too. Example 70: Omphale must tell Teukros that she has bought the painting herself (p. 208).

terms.def: Action of the mandator against the mandatarius for performance and surrender of what was obtained (p. 203).
Action of the mandatarius against the mandator for expenses and losses from executing the mandate; never for a fee (p. 204).
Gross negligence; together with DOLUS the usual limit of the mandatarius' liability (p. 206).

cards.q: What does the mandator claim with the ACTIO MANDATI DIRECTA?
cards.a:
Performance of the mandate and surrender of what the mandatarius obtained from the transaction (p. 203).
• Culpable non-performance: his expectation interest (p. 206)

cards.q: What does the mandatarius claim with the ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA?
cards.a:
Expenses and losses incurred in executing the mandate — never a fee (p. 204).
• Expenses: only those incurred BONA FIDE in duly performing it (Gaius D 17.1.27.4, Case 178)

cards.q: For which degree of fault is the mandatarius liable, and why?
cards.a:
As a rule only DOLUS and CULPA LATA (p. 206).
• Reason: a gratuitous act of friendship
• Principle of utility: liability follows the interests (p. 52)

cards.q: Example 66: Xerxes is to bring medicine from Greece for the sick Laura, breaks his leg and stays silent. Liable?
cards.a:
Yes. He breached his BONA FIDES duty to inform; not informing = CULPA LATA.
• Gaius D 17.1.27.2 (Case 185) (p. 206)

cards.q: What is the mandator's 'liability for risk'?
cards.a:
He must make good losses directly connected with executing the mandate, irrespective of his fault (p. 207).
• Reason: whoever benefits from the gratuitous performance carries the risk of accidental harm (p. 208)

cards.q: Example 69: on his way with Elektra's message Orestes is robbed of 100. Claim against Elektra?
cards.a:
No. Robbery, shipwreck and illness are the general risk of life, not a mandate-specific risk.
• Paulus D 17.1.26.6 (Case 179) (p. 208)

cards.q: Example 67: Bellona, asked to deliver a message, hires a horse although riding was not agreed. Can she recover the hire?
cards.a: No. Only expenses incurred in DULY performing the mandate are reimbursed; the horse was outside the mandate (p. 207).

cards.q: Example 70: Omphale asks Teukros to obtain a painting, then buys it herself. What must she do?
cards.a: Tell Teukros so that he stops trying: the mandator also has BONA FIDES secondary duties (protection, care, information) (p. 208).

4.title: Impossibility, exceeding the mandate, death
4.text:
The mandatarius must act as agreed. If that proves impossible, he must tell the mandator (p. 208).

### 1. Impossible without fault
The mandatarius is not liable. The mandator cannot demand performance but must reimburse the expenses incurred before the impossibility arose (p. 208). Example: the thing cannot be had at the agreed price. If the mandatarius buys it at a higher price, the mandator cannot demand delivery; if the mandatarius offers it at the higher price and the mandator accepts, that is a NEW contract (p. 209).

### 2. Possible, but not done as agreed
The mandatarius is liable for the mandator's interest (Gaius D 17.1.27.2, Case 185; Gai. 3.161, Case 183) (p. 209).

### 3. Exceeding the mandate: a school controversy
Gai. 3.161 (Case 183): E mandates T to buy land for 100,000 sesterces; T pays 150,000, although 100,000 would have been enough.
• Sabinians (Sabinus and Cassius, followed by Gaius): E has the ACTIO MANDATI for his interest. He MAY take the land, but need not; because T culpably breached the mandate, E can even refuse T's offer at 100,000. So T has no claim for his expenses if E does not want the land, even if T is willing to hand it over for 100,000 (p. 209).
• Proculians: if T hands the land over, he can recover the originally agreed price of 100,000 (Gaius D 17.1.4, Case 184/2; p. 210).
See model exegesis 2.

### 4. Death: MANDATUM MORTE SOLVITUR
The death of either party ends the mandate, because it is a highly personal relationship. Rights and duties under it do not pass to the heirs, unlike, e.g., a buyer's claim to delivery. Example 66: if Laura dies before Xerxes leaves for Greece, the contract lapses (p. 210). Exceptions:
• If execution has already begun, the mandator's heir reimburses the expenses already incurred, and gains from the execution go to the heirs.
• A mandatarius who carries out the mandate BONA FIDE without knowing of the mandator's death can claim his costs and losses with the ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA (Gai. 3.160, Case 186) (p. 210).

### Property-law twin
Exceeding authority also matters in property law: in Iavolenus D 39.5.25 an agent who donates in his own name instead of the owner's transfers no ownership (see section 2).

terms.def: The mandate ends with the death of either party, because it is highly personal (p. 210).
The mandatarius does what was possible but not as agreed, e.g. pays more than the set price; disputed between Sabinians and Proculians (Gai. 3.161; pp. 209–210).

cards.q: The mandate becomes impossible without the mandatarius' fault. Consequences?
cards.a:
He is not liable; the mandator cannot demand performance but must reimburse expenses incurred before the impossibility arose (p. 208).
• The mandatarius must notify the mandator

cards.q: The thing cannot be bought at the agreed price; the mandatarius buys it dearer. Can the mandator demand delivery?
cards.a: No. If the mandatarius offers it at the higher price and the mandator accepts, that is a new contract (p. 209).

cards.q: Gai. 3.161 (Case 183), Sabinian view: T, mandated to buy land for 100,000, pays 150,000. Position?
cards.a:
E may, but need not, take the land; T has no claim for expenses — even if he offers the land at 100,000.
• Sabinus and Cassius, followed by Gaius
• E has the ACTIO MANDATI for his interest (p. 209)

cards.q: Gai. 3.161: what is the Proculian view on exceeding the price limit?
cards.a:
If T hands the land over, he can recover the originally agreed 100,000.
• Gaius D 17.1.4 (Case 184/2) (p. 210)

cards.q: What does MANDATUM MORTE SOLVITUR mean, and why?
cards.a: The death of either party ends the mandate, because it is highly personal; rights and duties do not pass to the heirs (p. 210).

cards.q: What are the exceptions to MANDATUM MORTE SOLVITUR?
cards.a:
Execution already begun: the heir reimburses the expenses incurred, gains go to the heirs.
• A mandatarius acting BONA FIDE unaware of the death can claim costs and losses by ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA (Gai. 3.160, Case 186) (p. 210)

5.title: Loan mandate, surety, and transfer of claims
5.text:
### Loan mandate (MANDATUM PECUNIAE CREDENDAE)
Mandator A agrees with mandatarius B that B will lend money to C in B's OWN name and at B's OWN expense (p. 210). It is also called MANDATUM QUALIFICATUM. B must lend to C; A must make good B's loss if C does not repay. So it works like a guarantee (p. 211). Because the loan is made at B's expense, B cannot claim the whole sum lent as an 'expense' at once; he can claim from A only the loss if C fails to repay. 
Gai. 3.156 (Case 173): Ego urges Tu to lend out at interest money lying idle at home; the borrower does not pay. Ego is not liable: mere MANDATUM TUA GRATIA. Different if Tu is urged to lend to a SPECIFIC person, Titius, and agrees: that is a MANDATUM, and if Titius does not pay, Tu recovers from the mandator with the ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA. Controversy: Gaius follows Sabinus; Servius reportedly saw even this second case as mere advice (p. 211).

### Mandate and suretyship (useful for 16 Dec)
Whoever becomes surety at the debtor's request is his mandatarius and recovers his payment as an expense by the ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA (p. 277). Ulpian D 17.1.29.3 (Case 177): surety G pays the creditor without telling debtor D; D pays again. G has no claim: not informing comes very close to DOLUS (CULPA LATA); G may only demand that D assign to him D's CONDICTIO INDEBITI against the creditor (pp. 277–278). Without a mandate the relationship can be NEGOTIORUM GESTIO (p. 278).

### Changing the creditor: CESSIO, NOVATIO, MANDATUM IN REM SUAM
• An OBLIGATIO is a personal bond, so a claim cannot simply be transferred; a new creditor generally needs a NOVATIO by stipulation between him and the debtor, at the old creditor's request. Novation extinguishes the old obligation and its securities (pp. 212–213).
• MANDATUM AD AGENDUM IN REM SUAM: the creditor mandates the new creditor to sue the debtor; if it is agreed that he keeps the proceeds, this works like a cession, without the debtor's consent (p. 213).
• Weaknesses: the debtor can still pay the mandator; the mandator can revoke; the mandate ends on death. Imperial rescripts gave the PROCURATOR IN REM SUAM an ACTIO UTILIS (Gordianus C 4.10.1) (p. 214).

terms.def: Loan mandate (MANDATUM QUALIFICATUM): B lends to C in his own name and at his own expense on A's mandate; A covers B's loss if C does not repay (pp. 210–211).
Mandate to sue the debtor where the mandatarius keeps the proceeds; works like a transfer of the claim (p. 213).

cards.q: What is a loan mandate (MANDATUM PECUNIAE CREDENDAE)?
cards.a:
A mandates B to lend money to C in B's own name and at B's own expense; A must make good B's loss if C does not repay.
• Also MANDATUM QUALIFICATUM; works like a guarantee (pp. 210–211)

cards.q: Loan mandate: can the mandatarius claim the whole sum lent from the mandator as an 'expense'?
cards.a: No. The loan is made at his own expense; he can claim only the loss if the borrower fails to repay (p. 211).

cards.q: Gai. 3.156 (Case 173): advice to lend idle money at interest vs urging to lend to Titius — difference?
cards.a:
General advice = MANDATUM TUA GRATIA, no liability; to a specific person, accepted = MANDATUM, ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA if Titius defaults.
• Gaius follows Sabinus; Servius saw even the second as advice (p. 211)

cards.q: How does a surety who acted at the debtor's request recover what he paid?
cards.a:
As the debtor's mandatarius, by the ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA: the payment is an expense of the mandate (p. 277).
• Without a mandate: NEGOTIORUM GESTIO (p. 278)

cards.q: Ulpian D 17.1.29.3 (Case 177): surety G pays without telling debtor D, D pays again. Can G sue D?
cards.a:
No. Not informing comes very close to DOLUS (CULPA LATA).
• G can only demand that D assign him D's CONDICTIO INDEBITI against the creditor (pp. 277–278)

cards.q: What is a MANDATUM AD AGENDUM IN REM SUAM, and what are its weaknesses?
cards.a:
The creditor mandates the new creditor to sue and keep the proceeds: like a cession, without the debtor's consent (p. 213).
• Debtor can still pay the mandator; revocation; ends on death
• Rescripts: ACTIO UTILIS for the PROCURATOR IN REM SUAM (p. 214)

6.title: Mandate vs NEGOTIORUM GESTIO vs LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS
6.text:
All three can be about one person doing something for another. The book's revision question asks for exactly this comparison (p. 268). Ask two questions first: was there an AGREEMENT? Was a FEE agreed?

| | MANDATUM | NEGOTIORUM GESTIO | LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basis | Agreement (consensual contract) (p. 203) | NO mandate or other contract; a quasi-contract: duties arise from a contract-like factual situation (pp. 260–261) | Agreement (consensual contract) (p. 177) |
| Payment | Gratuitous; no fee (p. 204) | Gratuitous; origin in AMICITIA (p. 260) | Synallagmatic: a fee (MERCES) (p. 177) |
| What is owed | Manage another's affair (legal or factual act) as agreed | Manage another's affair; needs ANIMUS REM ALTERI GERENDI; for reimbursement ANIMUS RECIPIENDI (p. 262) | A result (OPUS) (p. 187) |
| Actions | ACTIO MANDATI DIRECTA / CONTRARIA (BONAE FIDEI) | ACTIO NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM DIRECTA / CONTRARIA (BONAE FIDEI) (p. 260) | ACTIO LOCATI (customer = LOCATOR) / ACTIO CONDUCTI (contractor = CONDUCTOR) |
| Liability of the person acting | DOLUS and CULPA LATA (p. 206) | OMNIS CULPA; only DOLUS in necessitous intervention; even chance losses for unusual transactions (pp. 265–266) | DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA for the customer's things; IMPERITIA counts as negligence (p. 187) |
| Expenses | Incurred BONA FIDE in duly performing; plus mandate-specific losses (p. 207) | Only if NEGOTIUM UTILITER GESTUM: judged by the principal's subjective interest, EX ANTE (UTILITER COEPTUM); necessary and useful, not luxury expenses (pp. 263–264) | Covered by the fee; payment risk by spheres (VITIUM OPERIS vs VITIUM SOLI, D 19.2.62) (p. 193) |
| Typical case | Buying a thing for a friend | Shoring up an absent neighbour's collapsing house (D 3.5.9(10).1, Case 219) | Launderer, transport of a column, building a canal |

### Points to remember
• A fee turns a mandate into a contract for work (p. 20).
• Without an agreement there is no mandate; NG may fill the gap. Both share the mixed-interest rule (p. 261).
• NG is judged by usefulness, because nobody asked the gestor to act. A mandatarius is reimbursed because he was asked, if he acted as asked.
• A surety's recourse is by mandate if he acted at the debtor's request, otherwise by NG (pp. 277–278).

terms.def: Deliberate management of another's affairs without a mandate or other contract; a quasi-contract (pp. 260–261).
Contract for work: production of a result (OPUS) for a fee (MERCES) (pp. 177, 187).
In NG it suffices that the management was usefully begun; usefulness is judged EX ANTE (p. 263).

cards.q: Mandate vs NEGOTIORUM GESTIO — what is the key difference?
cards.a:
Mandate rests on an agreement; in NG the gestor acts without a mandate or other contract (a quasi-contract).
• Both: gratuitous management of another's affairs, BONAE FIDEI actions (pp. 260–261)

cards.q: Mandate vs LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS — what is the key difference?
cards.a:
The fee: a mandate is gratuitous, a contract for work has a MERCES and owes a result (OPUS).
• Agreed fee = no longer a mandate (pp. 20, 177)

cards.q: Compare the standard of liability: mandatarius, NEGOTIORUM GESTOR, contractor (LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS).
cards.a:
Mandatarius: DOLUS + CULPA LATA; gestor: OMNIS CULPA; contractor: DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA.
• Gestor in necessitous intervention: only DOLUS (pp. 187, 206, 265–266)

cards.q: When can a NEGOTIORUM GESTOR recover his expenses, unlike a mandatarius?
cards.a:
Only if the management was useful (NEGOTIUM UTILITER GESTUM) for this principal, judged EX ANTE (UTILITER COEPTUM).
• Necessary and useful expenses, not luxury ones (pp. 263–264)

7.title: Mini exegesis 1: D 17.1.16 (Ravenna gardens, Case 175)
7.text:
Benke/Meissel Case 175 (p. 205). Read the text in Watson (vol. 2); the facts follow the book's summary.

### BASIC PART
1. Facts: Aurelius Quietus (Q) spends time every year in the gardens of his physician (P) at Ravenna. He asks P to build a ball court, steam baths and other health-promoting buildings there at Q's expense. P builds them.
2. Legal question: Can P recover his building costs from Q with the ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA, and to what extent?
3. Decision: The author is ULPIAN; he reports the opinion of CELSUS. P is reimbursed only insofar as the buildings did NOT raise the value of P's own property; only the excess of costs over the increase in value was spent purely in Q's interest (p. 205).

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. Institution: MANDATUM, the gratuitous management of another's affair on the basis of an agreement (p. 203). 'At Q's expense' is reimbursement, not a fee, so it is still a mandate (p. 20). The specific problem is the mandate in the COMMON interest of both parties (p. 205).
5. Claims: P v Q: reimbursement of his building costs. Basis: they are expenses incurred in carrying out the mandate (p. 204). Q v P: Q could demand that P build as agreed (ACTIO MANDATI DIRECTA) (not at issue).
6. Remedies: ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA, a BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM (p. 204).

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. Similar cases: NG between co-owners: Aron repairs the roof of the house he owns with Iokaste in equal shares and claims half from her (Example 80, p. 262); the mixed-interest rule is the same in NG (p. 261). For practice: Ex 56 (tenant Carus, owner Daphne, cost 15,000, increase in value 10,000, p. 216).
8. Controversies: none in the text; Celsus' view is reported without contradiction.
9. Dogmatic explanation: A mandate must concern ANOTHER'S affair. If it served only P, it would be no mandate at all (MANDATUM TUA GRATIA, p. 204). Here both are served: Q enjoys the facilities during his stays, but the buildings stand on P's land and, by SUPERFICIES SOLO CEDIT, belong to P (Property p. 137), so P's land is worth more. To that extent P built in his own interest. Only the costs beyond the increase in value were spent purely for Q, and only these are expenses 'of the mandate'. So P is not enriched at Q's cost, and the friend who acted gratuitously is still protected.

terms.def: A transaction in the common interest of mandator and mandatarius can be a mandate, but only insofar as the mandator's interest differs from the mandatarius' own (p. 205).

cards.q: Ulpian (Celsus) D 17.1.16 (Case 175): facts and legal question?
cards.a:
Quietus asks his physician to build a ball court and baths in the physician's gardens at Ravenna at Quietus' expense.
• Question: can the physician recover the costs with the ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA, and how much? (p. 205)

cards.q: D 17.1.16 (Case 175): what does Celsus decide, and why?
cards.a:
Reimbursement only insofar as the costs exceed the increase in value of the physician's own property.
• To that extent he built in his own interest; only the excess was spent purely for Quietus (p. 205)

cards.q: D 17.1.16: why do the buildings increase the physician's wealth and not Quietus'?
cards.a: They stand on the physician's land: SUPERFICIES SOLO CEDIT, so they belong to him (Property p. 137).

8.title: Mini exegesis 2: Gai. 3.161 (land bought too dear, Case 183)
8.text:
Benke/Meissel Case 183 (pp. 209–210), with Gaius D 17.1.4 (Case 184/2). Facts follow the book's summary.

### BASIC PART
1. Facts: E asks T to buy a piece of land for him for 100,000 sesterces. T buys it for 150,000, although he could have got it for 100,000.
2. Legal question: Must E take the land? Can T recover the price, or at least 100,000?
3. Decision: The author is GAIUS. E has the ACTIO MANDATI against T for his interest in correct performance. Following SABINUS and CASSIUS: E may, but need not, take the land; T has no claim for his expenses, even if he offers the land at 100,000. The PROCULIANS (Gaius D 17.1.4): if T hands the land over, he can recover the agreed 100,000 (pp. 209–210).

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. Institution: MANDATUM to buy (indirect agency). Problem: EXCEEDING the mandate, i.e. possible but not carried out as agreed (p. 209).
5. Claims: E v T: the land, if E wants it, or his interest (basis: T's culpable breach). T v E: the price as an expense of the mandate. Property: T bought in his own name, so he becomes possessor and, if the seller was authorised, owner; E gets the land only through a second transfer from T (Example 65, p. 205). E's right to the land is therefore only a claim, not a REI VINDICATIO.
6. Remedies: E: ACTIO MANDATI DIRECTA. T: ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA (Sabinians: fails; Proculians: up to 100,000 once T hands over).

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. Similar cases: the thing cannot be had at the agreed price, the mandatarius buys dearer: the mandator need not take it; acceptance at the higher price is a new contract (p. 209). Iavolenus D 39.5.25: an agent who exceeds his authority transfers no ownership (Property pp. 85–86). Practice: Ex 57 (p. 217).
8. Controversy: Sabinians (Sabinus, Cassius, Gaius) v Proculians.
9. Dogmatic explanation: The agreement defines what the mandatarius may do, and the mandator reimburses only expenses incurred in DULY performing the mandate (p. 207). The Sabinians treat any deviation as a breach that frees the mandator and leaves him the choice. The book calls it remarkable that T gets nothing even when he is willing to hand over at 100,000 (p. 209). The Proculians look at the result: if T hands over the land at the agreed price, E is exactly where the mandate would have put him, so refusing him would let E profit from T's mistake.

terms.def: The two classical law schools; in Gai. 3.161 they disagree on whether a mandatarius who paid more than the agreed price can recover at least the agreed price (pp. 209–210).

cards.q: Gai. 3.161 (Case 183): facts and legal question?
cards.a:
E mandates T to buy land for 100,000; T pays 150,000 although 100,000 would have sufficed.
• Question: must E take the land; can T recover the price or at least 100,000? (p. 209)

cards.q: Gai. 3.161: who owns the land after T buys it in his own name, and what does E have?
cards.a:
T (if the seller was authorised): indirect agency. E has only a contractual claim (ACTIO MANDATI DIRECTA), no REI VINDICATIO.
• E becomes owner only after a second transfer from T (Example 65, p. 205)

cards.q: Gai. 3.161: how can the Sabinian and the Proculian view be explained?
cards.a:
Sabinians: any deviation breaches the mandate; the mandator keeps his choice.
• Proculians: if T hands over at the agreed price, E gets exactly what he wanted, so T recovers 100,000 (pp. 209–210)

9.title: Mini exegesis 3: D 17.1.26.7 (the thieving slave, Case 182)
9.text:
Benke/Meissel Case 182 (p. 207), with Africanus (Julian) D 47.2.62(61).5 (Case 181). Read the text in Watson (vol. 2); the facts follow the book's summary and Example 68.

### BASIC PART
1. Facts: On B's mandate, A buys a slave for B. While the slave is staying with A, he steals from A.
2. Legal question: Must B make good A's loss with the ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA, and in full or only up to the value of the slave? Does it matter whether B knew that the slave was a thief?
3. Decision: The author is PAULUS; he cites NERATIUS. Neratius (and Paulus): B's liability can be limited to the value of the slave, by analogy to noxal liability. Paulus: if B KNEW the slave was a thief and did not warn A, B bears the WHOLE loss. In D 47.2.62(61).5, Africanus reports JULIAN: B bears the whole loss (p. 207).

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. Institution: MANDATUM; the MANDATOR'S liability for losses from carrying out the mandate (p. 207).
5. Claims: A v B: compensation for the stolen property. Basis: a loss directly linked to the mandate; the slave was in A's house only because A bought him for B. B: he did not know, so he owes at most the slave's value.
6. Remedies: ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA. Background: noxal liability means that the master of a slave who committed a delict may either pay compensation or surrender the slave (NOXAE DEDITIO) (p. 368).

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. Similar cases: in the paragraph just before (D 17.1.26.6, Case 179) robbery, shipwreck and illness are a general risk of life: no claim (p. 208). A seller whose runaway slave takes the buyer's property may surrender the slave instead of paying, under the NOXAE DEDITIO principle (p. 163). Practice: Ex 60 (p. 218).
8. Controversy: Neratius and Paulus (limit to the slave's value) v Julian (whole loss). All agree that the whole loss is owed if the mandator knew and failed to warn.
9. Dogmatic explanation: The mandator is liable for losses directly linked to the mandate, irrespective of fault: 'liability for risk' (p. 207). The reason is the principle of utility: the mandatarius acts gratuitously and only for the mandator, so whoever benefits from the performance should carry the risk of accidental harm (p. 208, citing the last sentence of D 47.2.62(61).5). Julian draws the full consequence; Neratius lets an innocent mandator owe no more than a slave's master owes in delict. Where the mandator knew and kept silent, he also breached his BONA FIDES duty to inform (p. 208), so there is no reason to protect him.

terms.def: Noxal surrender: the master of a slave who committed a delict may surrender the slave instead of paying compensation (pp. 163, 368).

cards.q: Paulus (Neratius) D 17.1.26.7 (Case 182): facts and legal question?
cards.a:
A buys a slave on B's mandate; while staying with A, the slave steals from A.
• Question: must B compensate A by the ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA — fully or only up to the slave's value? (p. 207)

cards.q: Slave bought on mandate steals from the mandatarius: what are the opinions?
cards.a:
Neratius (and Paulus): mandator may limit liability to the slave's value (analogy to noxal liability); Julian: whole loss.
• Whole loss in any case if the mandator knew and failed to warn (D 17.1.26.7; D 47.2.62(61).5) (p. 207)

cards.q: Why must the mandator bear losses of the mandatarius he did not cause (Julian's reasoning)?
cards.a:
Whoever benefits from the gratuitous performance should carry the risk of accidental harm (principle of utility).
• Africanus (Julian) D 47.2.62(61).5, last sentence (Case 181) (p. 208)

10.title: Exegesis checklist: a fragment on mandate
10.text:
Use the nine-step structure from the method lesson (EXME). For a mandate fragment, check these points.

### BASIC PART
1. Facts: Who asked whom to do what? Name MANDATOR and MANDATARIUS (A, B), and any third party (seller, borrower, creditor, debtor). Was there an AGREEMENT? Was a FEE agreed? Do not write legal conclusions into the facts.
2. Legal question: usually one of these: Is this a mandate at all? Can the mandatarius recover expenses or losses? Is the mandatarius liable? What is the effect of exceeding the mandate, of revocation or of death?
3. Decision: author from the INSCRIPTIO; separate the cited jurists (Celsus, Neratius, Julian, Sabinus/Cassius, Proculians) and say whether they give an opinion.

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. Institution: MANDATUM = consensual, gratuitous, imperfectly bilateral contract, BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM (pp. 203–204). Name the type: mandate to buy, loan mandate, mandate to stand surety, MANDATUM IN REM SUAM. Rule out CONSILIUM / MANDATUM TUA GRATIA, NEGOTIORUM GESTIO and LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS.
5. Claims in BOTH directions: mandator v mandatarius (performance, surrender of what was obtained, expectation interest); mandatarius v mandator (expenses incurred BONA FIDE in duly performing, mandate-specific losses; never a fee). Property side: who owns the thing bought? Remember indirect agency: the mandatarius acquires first (p. 205).
6. Remedies: ACTIO MANDATI DIRECTA / CONTRARIA; as BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA they allow set-off. Third parties, briefly: REI VINDICATIO and EXCEPTIO DOLI (Iavolenus D 39.5.25), CONDICTIO INDEBITI (D 17.1.29.3).

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. Similar cases: Examples 65–70; D 17.1.16; Gai. 3.161; D 17.1.26.6–7; Gai. 3.156; D 17.1.29.3.
8. Controversies: Sabinians v Proculians (exceeding, Gai. 3.161); Neratius/Paulus v Julian (thieving slave); Gaius/Sabinus v Servius (loan mandate, Gai. 3.156).
9. Dogmatic explanation: start from friendship and gratuitousness. They explain the MILD liability of the mandatarius (DOLUS, CULPA LATA) and the STRICT liability of the mandator for mandate-specific risks (principle of utility). Then: the agreement sets the limits; BONA FIDES adds duties to inform. Name the interests.

### Typical mistakes
• Giving the mandatarius a fee claim.
• Using OMNIS CULPA (that is NG) or CUSTODIA (that is LOCATIO CONDUCTIO) as the mandate standard.
• Letting the mandator vindicate a thing the mandatarius bought but has not yet transferred.
• Forgetting that the mandate ends with death (Gai. 3.160).

terms.def: Action whose INTENTIO refers to OPORTERE EX FIDE BONA; the ACTIO MANDATI is one (p. 204).

cards.q: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about a mandate — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.a:
Agreement and no fee? Another's affair (or CONSILIUM)? Claims both ways: performance v expenses/losses.
• Standard: mandatarius DOLUS + CULPA LATA; mandator liable for mandate-specific risk
• Exceeding, death, indirect agency (who owns the thing?)

cards.q: Which controversies on mandate should you know for an exegesis?
cards.a: Sabinians v Proculians on exceeding the price (Gai. 3.161); Neratius/Paulus v Julian on the thieving slave (D 17.1.26.7); Gaius/Sabinus v Servius on the loan mandate (Gai. 3.156).

cards.q: Name three typical mistakes in a mandate exegesis.
cards.a: A fee claim for the mandatarius; OMNIS CULPA or CUSTODIA as the mandate standard; letting the mandator vindicate a thing not yet transferred to him.
